book.title: Pneumonia, Sputum Retention and Airway Clearance
book.lead: Not every patient with pneumonia needs chest physiotherapy. Learn who does.

blocks.text: Pneumonia is infection of the lung tissue: alveoli fill with inflammatory fluid (consolidation). Consolidation is not sputum in the airways, so airway clearance techniques do not remove it. Physiotherapy helps when the patient has **sputum retention** (secretions they cannot clear), **atelectasis** (collapsed lung areas), reduced mobility, or deconditioning.

blocks.label: TEACHER'S VOICE
body: Ask three questions before chest physiotherapy: (1) Is there a problem I can treat (secretions, volume loss, immobility)? (2) Is the patient unable to clear it alone? (3) Will my technique change it? If all answers are no, focus on mobilisation and positioning, not airway clearance.

sections.title: B. Recognize problems physiotherapy can treat

rows: Coarse crackles, weak or ineffective cough, rattly breathing, rising oxygen needs
Reduced breath sounds at bases, dull percussion, low lung volumes after surgery or immobility

blocks.text: Cough strength and productivity; sputum colour, thickness, volume; pain limiting deep breaths; usual mobility; ability to follow instructions.
Vital signs and oxygen requirement; auscultation; cough assessment (peak cough flow if available); chest X-ray report; mobility assessment; ABG if available.

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Rising oxygen requirement, RR above about 30, confusion, falling BP
Desaturation during treatment not recovering with rest

blocks.text: Contraindications and precautions for airway clearance and head-down positions include: untreated pneumothorax, frank haemoptysis, recent head or eye surgery, raised intracranial pressure, severe reflux or aspiration risk, cardiovascular instability, and rib fractures for percussion [Ref – to verify local protocol].

steps: **Is the patient deteriorating?** Escalate to the medical team first.
**Sputum retention?** Airway clearance (ACBT, PEP, positioning, assisted cough, suction if needed and trained).
**Volume loss?** Positioning, deep breathing, incentive spirometry, mobilisation.
**Neither?** Mobilisation and positioning; no routine chest clearance.

rows: Upright sitting or side lying with the affected lung uppermost for drainage and ventilation
Sit out of bed, stand, walk
Increases lung volumes and secretion movement
3 to 4 slow deep breaths, hold 2 to 3 s
Breathing control, thoracic expansion exercises, forced expiration technique (huff)
Huff from mid-lung (medium breath, long huff) to high-lung (big breath, short huff)
Position the affected segment so gravity helps drainage
Head-down tilt only if no contraindication
Applied during expiration over the affected area
Adjunct; avoid over fractures, osteoporosis, low platelets
Firm pressure under the ribs or wound support during cough
When the patient cannot clear secretions

blocks.text: Progress from sitting out to walking, then to an exercise program before discharge if deconditioned. Older patients may need a structured rehabilitation pathway.
Auscultation, SpO2 and oxygen need, sputum clearance, RR, mobility level.

items: **Does airway clearance remove consolidation?** No. Consolidation is inside the alveoli; airway clearance targets secretions in the airways.
**What is the best single intervention for many pneumonia patients?** Early mobilisation and upright positioning.
**Describe a huff.** A forced but open-glottis expiration, like fogging a mirror.
**Name two contraindications to head-down drainage.** Raised intracranial pressure and severe reflux or aspiration risk.
**What sign suggests sputum retention?** Coarse crackles with a weak, ineffective cough.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Decide when chest physiotherapy is indicated.
Perform ACBT, positioning and assisted cough.
